title: Testing a fire detection and alarm system in an occupied building
verdict:
I would not sign this yet, but it is close, and the reason is not the law — it is two ceiling-level killers the document does not control.

WHAT I VERIFIED AND FOUND CORRECT (do not "fix" these):
• Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) — I pulled SL 2026 No. 113 in full. Every section the SWMS cites is real and says what the SWMS says it says: s 193 ("near ... means within 3m of an exposed energised part"), s 195(1)(a)-(d) (the four circumstances, verbatim), s 196(1), s 199(1)(a)-(e) (recorded risk assessment, s 200 SWMS, clear work area, isolation point clearly marked/labelled and capable of being operated quickly, authorisation after consulting the person with management or control), s 200 (contents), s 201, s 202, s 203(1)(c) safety observer, s 203(3) testing exemption ("the work consists only of testing" AND "a risk assessment ... shows there is no serious risk"), s 204, and s 211 ("competent in rescue and resuscitation in accordance with recognised practices in the electricity industry"). The 2013→2026 rewrite was done properly. No dead citation survives.
• WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) — all six hrcw paragraphs are verbatim, including s 291(a) "involves a risk of a person falling more than 2m". s 289(2)(e), s 289(3)(d), s 292 ($250,000), s 299(4) (which does exist, and does say "including by addressing the general fall protection requirements in section 79(3)"), s 300 (arrangements + stop work, no signature duty — the document is right to say so), s 301 (construction project only), ss 78(3), 79(3)(a)-(c), 80(2)-(4), s 48(2), ss 56/57/58, ss 425/427, sch 19 "fall arrest system". All confirmed.
• Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) is still in force (SL 2008 No. 160). s 19, s 49 (including the worked example "a defect making a fire detection and alarm system inoperable"), s 50, s 53 ("within 24 hours after the person carries out the maintenance" — the document's emphasis is exactly right), s 54(4), s 55(2)-(3), s 55A(3). All confirmed.
• Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) — correct current name; ch 4A pt 6 "Charges for services" confirmed, and s 148Z is titled "Person for whose benefit service provided is liable for charge", which is precisely what the emergency section asserts. s 150B "False calls" confirmed.
• Standards — checked against the Standards Australia catalogue record. AS 1670.1:2024, AS 1670.3:2024 and AS 1670.4:2024 all exist, all published 28 Jun 2024, all Current, and AS 1670.1:2024 does supersede the 2018 edition. AS 1851-2012 + Amd 1:2016, AS 4214:2018 + Amd 1:2019, AS/NZS 3000:2018, AS/NZS 2865:2009, AS/NZS 1891.1:2020, AS/NZS 1891.4:2025, AS 1892.1:2018, AS 1892.5:2020, AS/NZS 1269.3:2005, AS/NZS 1270:2002, AS/NZS 1337.1:2010, AS 2210.3:2019, AS 1674.1:2025 — every number and edition is real and current.
• All eight Codes of Practice exist under those exact titles on worksafe.qld.gov.au, including the awkward one: "Electrical Safety Code of Practice 2021 - Managing electrical risks in the workplace".
• Shape: all twelve keys present, no extras, no suggestFor. Controls are in hierarchy order in all twelve steps. No residualRisk exceeds its initialRisk. No step is admin/PPE-only with a low residual.

WHAT STOPS THE SIGNATURE:
Step 7 names "contact with a live luminaire, busway or a sprinkler head while reaching" as a hazard and then never controls it. That step's own eliminate control sends a technician up a telescopic pole into that exact space. Electrocution off a busway and a sheared sprinkler head in an occupied data hall are both live outcomes with nothing written against them.

And the SWMS makes an EWP its preferred fall prevention device for ceiling-height work in an occupied building, which is the single environment where EWP operators are crushed between the basket and an overhead beam or ceiling. That word appears nowhere in the document.

Both are the kind of thing an author who has controlled falls, gas discharge and 240V very well simply did not look up at. Fix those two, add the scaffold controls, correct the BFSR part number, and I would sign it and send a crew out on it.

blocking.field: steps[6] (step 7 'Test detectors, manual call points and beam, duct or aspirating devices') — hazards[2] has no matching entry in controls[]
blocking.problem: The hazard 'Contact with a live luminaire, busway or a sprinkler head while reaching' is named and then abandoned. Nothing in the fourteen controls addresses electrical clearance at ceiling level or protection of sprinkler heads. Worse, controls[0] (eliminate) directs the technician to 'Test from floor level with a telescopic test pole' — poles for this work are commonly aluminium, and the document sends one up into the same ceiling space it has just identified as containing exposed busway and live luminaires, with no clearance rule and no requirement for a non-conductive pole. A sheared sprinkler head over an occupied data hall or a stage is a major-loss event; contact with a busway from a metal pole, a ladder or an EWP basket is a fatality.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].controls, placed with the other engineering/administrative controls in hierarchy order: (engineering) 'Non-conductive (fibreglass or composite) test pole only. No metal pole is taken into a ceiling space that contains busway, open luminaire terminals or unsheathed services.' (administrative) 'Before the pole, the ladder or the EWP goes up, look at what is at head height at that device: busway, open luminaire terminations, unsheathed cable, sprinkler heads and pipework. Where an exposed energised part cannot be avoided, that is work near energised electrical equipment — stop, and it goes to the licensed electrical worker under the separate ESR 2026 s 200 SWMS, not to a fire technician with a pole.' (administrative) 'Sprinkler heads: identify every head within reach of the pole, the ladder or the basket before you start, keep the pole and the basket clear of heads and pipework, and never use a head or a pipe as a hand-hold or to steady yourself. A struck head discharges immediately — if one is knocked, get clear, tell the FM, and the sprinkler contractor isolates the affected zone.' Note that the obligation to keep clear of energised parts is in the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld), Part 8 Division 3 — cite s 193's 3m 'near' definition only, which is already confirmed elsewhere in this document; do not invent a clause for the sprinkler control.

blocking.field: steps[6].hazards and steps[6].controls[4] (the EWP engineering control); also whenRequired, the falls hierarchy item 3
blocking.problem: The SWMS makes an EWP the preferred fall prevention device for work at ceiling height in an occupied building, and never once names crush or entrapment between the basket and the overhead structure. That is the dominant EWP fatality mechanism in exactly this environment — a technician working overhead, looking up at a detector, operating the up control, and pinning himself between the basket rail or the control panel and a beam, a duct, a pipe run or the slab soffit. There is no control for secondary guarding, no rule to keep the body inside the basket and clear of the overhead line of travel, no requirement that a second person on the ground knows and has demonstrated the emergency lowering controls before the basket leaves the floor, and no rule about elevating only in short increments in a low ceiling. The document mentions 'EWP ground controls proven working' once, but only as a rescue means for a suspended-harness casualty in steps[6].controls[11], not as a crush rescue. Machine stability is likewise unaddressed in the step: whenRequired mentions floor loading as a reason to reject an EWP, but steps[6] carries no control for level firm ground, outriggers/stabilisers deployed, or travelling elevated.
blocking.fix: Add 'Crush or entrapment between the EWP basket and an overhead beam, duct, pipe run or ceiling slab' and 'EWP overturn on a soft, sloping or overloaded floor' to steps[6].hazards. Add to steps[6].controls, in hierarchy order beside the existing EWP control: (engineering) 'EWP fitted with secondary guarding (an anti-entrapment bar or pressure-sensing device) wherever one is available for the machine type on hire — specify it at the hire order, not at the site.' (administrative) 'Before the basket is elevated, look up and identify the overhead obstruction directly above the line of travel. In a low or cluttered ceiling, elevate in short increments, keep the whole body inside the basket and never lean over the controls, and stop elevating a full arm's length short of the obstruction.' (administrative) 'A second person stays at ground level for the whole time the basket is up, has been shown the emergency lowering controls and has operated them once before the machine is used, and can lower the basket without help.' (administrative) 'EWP set on level firm floor within its rated capacity, stabilisers or outriggers deployed where fitted, never travelled elevated except where the machine is rated for it and the route has been walked. Confirm the floor loading with the FM before a machine goes onto a suspended slab or over a basement.' Add a matching siteSpecificPrompt: 'If an EWP is used today — what is directly overhead at each device, is secondary guarding fitted, who is the ground person, and have they operated the emergency lowering controls?'

blocking.field: steps[6].controls[4] (the mobile scaffold engineering control), and training[]
blocking.problem: The SWMS offers 'a mobile scaffold with guardrails' as a primary fall prevention device under s 79(3)(a) and then gives the crew nothing to work to. There is no control for castors locked before anyone climbs, outriggers or stabilisers deployed, platform height to base ratio, access from inside the frame, nobody on the platform while it is moved, and no check that the floor is level and clear along the move route. Nor is there any competency requirement: training[] carries RIIWHS204E, EWPA Yellow Card and the WP high risk work licence, but nothing for scaffolding. In a warehouse, dock or atrium — exactly the buildings this SWMS names — a mobile scaffold at detector height will exceed the threshold at which erecting, altering or dismantling it is licensed work. WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld), schedule 19 defines scaffolding work as 'erecting, altering or dismantling a temporary structure that is or has been erected to support a platform and from which a person or object could fall more than 4m from the platform or the structure', and s 81 with schedule 3 makes Basic scaffolding a licensed class of high risk work. A crew reading this document would erect a scaffold unlicensed and move it with a technician on the deck.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].controls, immediately after the existing engineering control: (engineering) 'Mobile scaffold: castors locked and outriggers or stabilisers deployed before anyone climbs; guardrails and toeboards fitted on all sides; access up the internal ladder, never the outside of the frame; platform height within the manufacturer''s height-to-base ratio for that unit; nobody and nothing on the deck while it is moved, and the move route walked for level floor, floor penetrations and overhead services first.' Add to training[]: 'Basic scaffolding high risk work licence (SB) where a mobile scaffold is erected, altered or dismantled and a person or object could fall more than 4m from the platform or structure — WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 81 and schedule 3; see the schedule 19 definition of scaffolding work. Under that height, competence to the manufacturer''s instructions and Safe QLD''s mobile scaffold procedure.' Add a siteSpecificPrompt asking whether the scaffold height at any device puts the job over the 4m licensed threshold.

blocking.field: steps[0].controls[2].control (step 1, 'Get the site's fire and evacuation plan (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld), part 3)')
blocking.problem: Wrong part. I pulled the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld), SL 2008 No. 160, current version. Part 3 is headed 'Occupancy limits for buildings' and contains s 14 'Meaning of occupancy safety factors' and the occupancy-limit provisions — nothing about fire and evacuation plans. Evacuation planning is Part 4, headed 'Evacuation planning, instruction and practice', which is also where s 17 'Meaning of evacuation coordination procedures', s 18 'Meaning of evacuation diagram' and s 19 'Meaning of person with special needs' — the section this SWMS correctly relies on in step 8 — actually sit. A technician or an FM sent to part 3 for the fire and evacuation plan finds occupancy limits.
blocking.fix: Change 'Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld), part 3' to 'Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld), part 4'. Everything else in that control is fine.

blocking.problem: The edition number and year are right but the title belongs to the superseded edition. The Standards Australia catalogue record for AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 (published 28 Aug 2020, status Current) gives the title 'Personal equipment for work at height, Part 1: Manufacturing requirements for full body combination and lower body harnesses'. 'Industrial fall-arrest systems and devices, Part 1: Harnesses and ancillary equipment' is the title of AS/NZS 1891.1:2007, which the catalogue shows as Available Superseded. The document has paired the 2020 number with the 2007 name.
blocking.fix: Change references[26] to: 'AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 Personal equipment for work at height, Part 1: Manufacturing requirements for full body combination and lower body harnesses, and AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 Personal equipment for work at height, Part 4: Selection, use and maintenance'. The 1891.4:2025 half is already correct — published 19 Sep 2025, Current.

blocking.field: references[31] ('AS 2210.3:2019 Occupational protective footwear — Specification for safety footwear')
blocking.problem: Same fault as the 1891 entry: right number and year, superseded title. The catalogue record for AS 2210.3:2019 (published 14 May 2019, Current) gives 'Personal protective equipment, Part 3: Safety footwear (ISO 20345:2011, MOD)'. 'Occupational protective footwear, Part 3: Specification for safety footwear' is AS/NZS 2210.3:2009, which the catalogue shows as Superseded by AS 2210.3:2019. The same wording appears in ppe[4] ('Safety footwear to AS 2210.3'), which is fine because it carries no title.
blocking.fix: Change references[31] to 'AS 2210.3:2019 Personal protective equipment, Part 3: Safety footwear (ISO 20345:2011, MOD)'. Leave ppe[4] as it is.

blocking.field: references[9] ('Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) — chapter 4A, part 6 charges for services (ss 148X–150) ...')
blocking.problem: The section range overshoots the part. In the current Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld), chapter 4A part 6 'Charges for services' runs from s 148X 'Definitions for part' to s 149G. Section 149H 'Authorised fire officers' opens chapter 4B part 1, and s 150 sits inside chapter 4B, not in the charges part. The part reference itself is right, and the substantive claim in the emergency section is right — s 148Z is headed 'Person for whose benefit service provided is liable for charge' and says exactly that — so only the bracketed range is wrong. s 150B 'False calls' is correctly cited on its own.
blocking.fix: Change '(ss 148X–150)' to '(ss 148X–149G)', or drop the range and leave 'chapter 4A, part 6 (Charges for services)'.

blocking.field: permits[6] ('... the written rescue plan that WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 80 requires')
blocking.problem: Overstates the section. WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 80 requires the PCBU to 'establish emergency procedures, including rescue procedures' (s 80(2)), to 'ensure that the emergency procedures are tested so that they are effective' (s 80(3)), and to 'provide relevant workers with suitable and adequate information, training and instruction in relation to the emergency procedures' (s 80(4)). It nowhere requires the procedures to be in writing. Making a written plan the rule is good practice and Safe QLD should keep it, but attributing the writing requirement to s 80 is the same failure mode this document warns about elsewhere. steps[6].controls[11] states it correctly and should be the model.
blocking.fix: Reword permits[6] to: '... and, where fall arrest may be used, Safe QLD's written rescue plan for that location — Safe QLD's standard for the emergency and rescue procedures that WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 80 requires to be established, tested so they are effective, and trained — on site before anyone clips on.' Same correction in ppe[9], which repeats the phrasing.

blocking.field: steps[8].controls[3] (step 9, 'Prove one output at a time, watch the plant actually respond, and reset it before moving to the next')
blocking.problem: Labelled 'engineering' when it is a work-sequencing procedure — an administrative control by any reading. It depends entirely on the technician choosing to do it in that order; nothing in the plant enforces it. Sitting above the administrative block, it inflates the apparent strength of the controls on a step whose hazards are lift, shutter and damper crush injuries. The step's residual of medium is still carried by the three genuine isolate controls, so nothing downstream breaks — but the label is wrong and a regulator reading the hierarchy will pick it. (controls[4], the shutter control, is defensible as engineering because the barricade is a physical barrier.)
blocking.fix: Change steps[8].controls[3].level from 'engineering' to 'administrative' and move it to the top of the administrative block, immediately before the current controls[5] ('Call and response with the person watching the far end'). Order within the step then stays valid.

blocking.field: steps[2].controls[6] (step 3, 'Ring the fire monitoring centre (Johnson Controls for QFD-monitored ASEs ...)' and the 'QFD OM129' form number)
blocking.problem: Two operational facts I could not verify against a QFD publication: that Johnson Controls is the monitoring centre for QFD-monitored ASEs, and that the ASE isolation request form is 'QFD OM129'. The QFD site does not carry a reachable alarm-isolation page to confirm either. The control does hedge ('confirm this site's centre on the job before you ring'), and permits[1] refers generically to 'the monitoring contractor's isolation request form', so the crew has a fallback. But a form number is exactly the sort of detail people copy without checking, and an isolation request lodged on a superseded form number goes nowhere — which means the brigade signal is not isolated on the day and the first detector test turns out appliances.
blocking.fix: Either confirm the current form number and monitoring provider directly with QFD or the site's monitoring contractor before this template is issued, or soften it to: 'Where the panel cannot be isolated locally, the monitoring contractor's current ASE isolation request form goes to them ahead of the day, not on the morning — confirm the current form and the site's monitoring centre with QFD or the contractor before you lodge it.' Add a siteSpecificPrompt asking which monitoring centre holds this site and which isolation form they are currently accepting.
